newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Cholera fears as Rwanda refugee airlift to start.
newsitem.headline: Cholera fears as Rwanda refugee airlift to start.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency said on Wednesday an airlift of Rwandan refugees in Zaire would start on Friday but the local governor said it could be delayed by cholera.
"We have asked for permission to begin on Friday and the (rebel) Alliance has agreed and so we are planning to begin on Friday," said UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg in Kisangani.
"The first group to be flown out will be 80 unaccompanied minors who are in decent health and can travel," he added.
The United Nations plans to airlift some 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees via Kisangani to the eastern Zairean border city of Goma, from where they will be repatriated by truck to Rwanda.
But the newly-elected governor of rebel-held Upper Zaire said he feared a cholera outbreak among the Hutu refugees could spread to the Zairean population if the operation gets underway.
"Frankly, it is not our wish to start the operation with cholera in the camps, to bring refugees into the town on Friday," Governor Yagi Sitolo told Reuters before meeting a UNHCR official.

"I would rather that they don't start while there is still cholera in the camps. Why take the risk of bringing cholera into the city?" he said. Kisangani, a city of one million and the capital of northwest Zaire, was seized by rebels on March 15.
UNHCR officials have said the 150 cholera cases and nine deaths of refugees so far in camps south of Kisangani should not impede the start of the airlift as only healthy refugees would be flown out.
The operation would be one of the largest airlifts of refugees ever and is expected to cost millions of dollars.
A Zairean official of the World Health Organisation (WHO) announced the epidemic on Sunday after five cholera deaths in Kasese 2 refugee site, 29 km (17 miles) south of Kisangani.
An estimated 50,000 Rwandan refugees are camped out at Kasese with a similar number in makeshift camps further south.
WHO official Leonard Kinuani said on Sunday the epidemic was certain to delay repatriating the refugees, who stopped months of trekking eastwards after rebels overran the area south of Kisangani.
But UNHCR says it appears to be a non-virulent strain which is not particularly communicable and the camps are stabilising.

The refugees are the rump of more than two million Rwandan Hutus who fled their country in July 1994 after the victory of Tutsi rebels in the civil war and the genocide of 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
Most returned home late last year but about 300,000 are believed to be stranded in Zaire, with the largest concentration between Kisangani and Ubundi, 125 km (75 miles) to the south.

Rebel chief Laurent Kabila came under international pressure this month to agree to the airlift after earlier insisting the refugees should be trucked home, though the roads are impassable for long stretches.

The refugees are in a very poor state after trekking about 600 km (375 miles) since last October through dense jungle where they survived on grubs and tree-bark. They marched westwards to flee Tutsi-dominated rebels, supported by Rwanda's government.
